To analyze mathematical models involving exponential and logarithmic functions in greater detail, we need to develop rules for computing the derivative of these functions. We begin by looking at the rule for computing the derivative of the exponential function.

section.paragraph: Thus, the derivative of the exponential function with base $$e$$ is equal to the function itself. To demonstrate the validity of this rule, we compute

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{e^{x + h} - e^{x}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{e^{x}\left( {e^{h} - 1} \right)}{h} { \text{Write} e^{x + h} = e^{x}e^{h} \text{and factor} .}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {e^{x}\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{e^{h} - 1}{h}} \text{Why?} } \end{array}$$
To evaluate
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{e^{h} - 1}{h}$$

list.item: The Product Rule gives $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({x^{2}e^{x}})} = x^{2}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(e^{x})} + e^{x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{2})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {x^{2}e^{x} + e^{x}\left( {2x} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = xe^{x}\left( {x + 2} \right)} \end{array}$$ Algebra See Example 7.

Using the General Power Rule, we find $$\begin{array}{l} {g^{\prime}{(t)} = \frac{3}{2}{({e^{t} + 2})}^{1 \slash 2}\frac{d}{\mathit{dt}}{({e^{t} + 2})}} \\ {\phantom{g^{\prime}{(t)}} = \frac{3}{2}{({e^{t} + 2})}^{1 \slash 2}e^{t} = \frac{3}{2}e^{t}{({e^{t} + 2})}^{1 \slash 2}} \end{array}$$
Use the definition of the derivative of a function to show that $$f^{\prime}(x) = b^{x} \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{b^{h} - 1}{h}$$

Use the result of part 1 to show that $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( 2^{x} \right)} & = & {2^{x} \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{2^{h} - 1}{h}} \\ {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( 3^{x} \right)} & = & {3^{x} \cdot \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{3^{h} - 1}{h}} \end{array}$$
Use the technique in Using Technology, to show that (to two decimal places) $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{2^{h} - 1}{h} = 0.69$$ and $$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{3^{h} - 1}{h} = 1.10$$

Conclude from the results of parts 2 and 3 that $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( 2^{x} \right) \approx (0.69)2^{x}$$ and $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( 3^{x} \right) \approx (1.10)3^{x}$$ Thus, $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( b^{x} \right) = k \cdot b^{x}$$ where $$k$$ is an appropriate constant.

The results of part 4 suggest that, for convenience, we pick the base $$b$$ , where $$2 < b < 3$$ , so that $$k = 1$$ . This value of $$b$$ is $$e \approx 2.718281828\ldots$$ . Thus, $$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{x} \right) = e^{x}$$ This is why we prefer to work with the exponential function $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ .

section.heading: Applying the Chain Rule to Exponential Functions
section.paragraph: To enlarge the class of exponential functions to be differentiated, we appeal to the Chain Rule to obtain the following rule for differentiating composite functions of the form $$h(x) = e^{f{(x)}}$$ . An example of such a function is $$h(x) = e^{x^{2} - 2x}$$ . Here, $$f(x) = x^{2} - 2x$$ .
